Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Radium and polonium (Curie): Marie Curie's second Nobel, and she named polonium after her native Poland, which was not an independent country at the time.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Ammonia synthesis (Haber): Haber's process pulls nitrogen from air to make fertilizer that helps feed about half of humanity, though he also pioneered chemical weapons.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Artificial radioactivity: Irene Joliot-Curie and her husband Frederic made radioactive elements in the lab, and she was Marie Curie's daughter.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Radiocarbon dating: Willard Libby's method measures carbon-14 in organic remains, and can date material up to roughly 50,000 years old.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.X-ray structures (Hodgkin): Dorothy Hodgkin used X-ray crystallography to solve the structure of penicillin, vitamin B12 and later insulin.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.PCR: Kary Mullis reportedly conceived this DNA-copying method on a night drive, and it later underpinned COVID tests.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Buckyballs: The soccer-ball-shaped carbon molecule C60 was named after architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes it resembles.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Lithium-ion batteries: John Goodenough became the oldest Nobel laureate in history at 97, and the batteries power phones and electric cars.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.CRISPR gene editing: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna were the first all-female pair to win a science Nobel for these molecular scissors.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry: when these wer.Quantum dots: These nanocrystals glow in a color set by their size, and are used in some TVs and displays.

When these world weather records were se.Wettest year (Cherrapunji): That year Cherrapunji, India, got over 26 meters of rain, a record that still stands, and it remains one of the wettest places on Earth.
When these world weather records were se.Hottest air (Death Valley): The record 56.7 °C (134 °F) at Furnace Creek is still officially the hottest air temperature ever recorded, though some experts dispute it.
When these world weather records were se.Mt Washington wind gust: A 231 mph (372 km/h) gust at this New Hampshire peak stood for 62 years as the highest wind speed measured at the surface.
When these world weather records were se.Most rain in 24 hrs (Réunion): Tropical Cyclone Denise dumped about 1.8 meters of rain on the island in a single day.
When these world weather records were se.Highest air pressure (Siberia): Super-cold, dense Siberian winter air pushed the pressure to about 1,084 hPa, the highest ever recorded at sea level.
When these world weather records were se.Lowest pressure (Typhoon Tip): The storm's pressure of 870 hPa is the lowest ever measured at sea level, and it was also the largest tropical cyclone on record, about 2,200 km wide.
When these world weather records were se.Coldest air (Vostok): Antarctica's -89.2 °C (-128.6 °F) is the coldest air temperature measured at ground level, though satellites have seen colder surface spots.
When these world weather records were se.Strongest gust (Barrow Island): Tropical Cyclone Olivia whipped up a 408 km/h gust, the strongest wind ever measured that was not from a tornado.
When these world weather records were se.Fastest tornado winds: Doppler radar clocked winds of about 480 km/h in an Oklahoma tornado, the fastest wind speeds ever measured on Earth.
When these world weather records were se.Biggest US hailstone: The 8-inch-wide hailstone that fell in Vivian, South Dakota, is the largest recorded in the US, weighing nearly 2 pounds.

The size of these ancient structures.Stonehenge sarsen circle: Its sarsen stones weigh about 25 tons each, and the smaller bluestones were hauled from Wales, some 250 km away.
The size of these ancient structures.Pantheon dome: It remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, topped by an open oculus about 8 metres wide.
The size of these ancient structures.Parthenon: Its columns lean slightly inward and bulge, subtle refinements that correct optical illusions.
The size of these ancient structures.Hagia Sophia: Finished in 537 under Justinian in about five years, it was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.
The size of these ancient structures.Colosseum: A retractable awning, the velarium, was operated by sailors to shade the crowd.
The size of these ancient structures.Great Pyramid: Built for Khufu around 2560 BC, it was the tallest man-made structure for about 3,800 years.
The size of these ancient structures.Pont du Gard: This Roman aqueduct bridge in France was built without mortar to carry water to Nimes.
The size of these ancient structures.Circus Maximus: This racetrack in Rome could reportedly hold around 150,000 spectators.
The size of these ancient structures.Trajan's Bridge, Danube: Built by Apollodorus of Damascus, it was the longest arch bridge for around a thousand years.
The size of these ancient structures.Hadrian's Wall: Begun in 122 AD, it crosses England's neck from the Tyne to the Solway Firth and is a UNESCO site.

How many? Toes, teats and more.Toes on a horse's foot: A horse's single toe ends in a hoof, the evolved middle toe, and the knee we see is actually its wrist.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Toes on a camel's foot: Camels walk on two toes with wide pads that spread their weight on soft sand.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Toes on a rhino's foot: Rhinos belong to the odd-toed ungulates, along with horses and tapirs.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Toes on a hippo's foot: Hippos have four toes with hoof-like nails and walk along river bottoms rather than swim.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Fingers on a gorilla's hand: Gorillas walk on their knuckles, and each has a unique nose print.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Legs on a spider: Spiders sense vibrations and smells through hairs on their legs.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Teats on a sow: Sows commonly bear litters of ten or more piglets.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Vertebrae in a human spine: Humans are born with 33 vertebrae, and the lowest ones fuse into the sacrum and tailbone.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Spines on a hedgehog: The spines are hollow modified hairs, and a hedgehog rolls into a ball when threatened.
How many? Toes, teats and more.Feathers on a tundra swan: This famous count has most of its feathers on the head and neck.

How long these events last.Rodeo bull ride: A rodeo rider must stay on a bull for 8 seconds, which is long enough that fewer than half of riders succeed.
How long these events last.Olympic 100 m final: The 100 meters final lasts less than ten seconds, and a sprinter takes about 45 strides.
How long these events last.Elite mile race: An elite mile race is just under four minutes for men, a barrier first broken by Roger Bannister in 1954.
How long these events last.Rugby union match: A rugby union match is 80 minutes, in two halves of 40, and the clock keeps running unless a referee stops it.
How long these events last.Pro round of golf: A pro round of golf takes about four hours, and a player may walk about five miles.
How long these events last.Le Mans race: Le Mans is a 24-hour race, where teams of drivers share cars, and the winner is who covers the most distance.
How long these events last.Test cricket match: Test cricket can last up to five days and still end in a draw, which is a strange thing for many other sports fans.
How long these events last.Wimbledon: Wimbledon is played over two weeks and has strict dress code, which is mostly all white.
How long these events last.Tour de France: The Tour de France covers over 3,000 km in three weeks, and has stages in the mountains and an ending on the Champs-Élysées.
How long these events last.Vendee Globe (winner): The Vendée Globe is a solo race around the world without stops or help, and the winner takes around 80 days.

Shortest stints at the top.Leroy Rosenior, Torquay boss: He was sacked at Torquay United in 2007 after about ten minutes in the job, when new owners took over the club.
Shortest stints at the top.Pedro Lascuráin, Mexico: In 1913 he held Mexico's presidency for under an hour, in a coup deal that handed power to General Huerta.
Shortest stints at the top.Lady Jane Grey: The Nine Days' Queen of 1553 was beheaded the following year at about 16 or 17 years old.
Shortest stints at the top.Pope Urban VII: He died of malaria before he could even be crowned, but not before decreeing the first known public ban on smoking, in churches.
Shortest stints at the top.William Henry Harrison: He gave the longest inaugural speech in US history, then died a month later, possibly of typhoid rather than the pneumonia long blamed on the cold.
Shortest stints at the top.Pope John Paul I: Known as the Smiling Pope, his sudden death in 1978 sparked conspiracy theories and led to John Paul II, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years.
Shortest stints at the top.Liz Truss: Her time was so brief that in 2022 a newspaper's livestream of a head of lettuce was said to outlast her.
Shortest stints at the top.Sam Allardyce, England boss: He was out after a newspaper sting in 2016, having managed just one match, a 1-0 win over Slovakia.
Shortest stints at the top.King Edward V: One of the Princes in the Tower, the boy vanished in 1483 after his uncle took the throne as Richard III.
Shortest stints at the top.George Canning, UK PM: He was the shortest-serving UK prime minister until Truss, because he died in office in 1827.

Highest pitch they can hear.Goldfish: Tiny Weberian bones link its swim bladder to the inner ear, extending its hearing beyond that of many other fish.
Highest pitch they can hear.Elephant: They also pick up very low rumbles, called infrasound, partly through their feet.
Highest pitch they can hear.Human: Hearing declines with age, and many adults can no longer hear above about 15 kHz, which is why mosquito ringtones work on teens.
Highest pitch they can hear.Horse: Its ears can rotate nearly 180 degrees, each independently.
Highest pitch they can hear.Dog: Dog whistles work because dogs hear well above the human range.
Highest pitch they can hear.Cat: It can hear the squeaks of mice, which are high-pitched, which helps make it an excellent hunter.
Highest pitch they can hear.Rat: Rats giggle in ultrasound when tickled, in sounds humans cannot hear.
Highest pitch they can hear.Mouse: Males sing ultrasonic courtship songs that humans cannot hear.
Highest pitch they can hear.Bottlenose dolphin: Its echolocation clicks bounce off prey, and sound reaches its ear mainly through the lower jaw.
Highest pitch they can hear.Greater wax moth: It has the highest hearing known in any animal, probably as a defense against bat echolocation.

Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Triumphal entry: Mark mentions people spreading cloaks and leafy branches on the road; the palms of Palm Sunday come from John's Gospel.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Cleansing the Temple: He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of dove sellers, saying the house of prayer had become a den of robbers.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Judas agrees to betray: Mark gives no price for the betrayal; the famous thirty pieces of silver appear only in Matthew's Gospel.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Last Supper: The meal was a Passover supper and is the origin of the Eucharist, which many Christians still celebrate in memory of it.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Prayer in Gethsemane: The name Gethsemane means oil press in Aramaic, and it was a garden on the Mount of Olives, where olive trees still grow.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Arrest of Jesus: Judas identified Jesus to the crowd with a kiss, a signal agreed in advance because it was dark and the guards did not know him by sight.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Peter's denials: A rooster crows, as Jesus had predicted, after the third denial, and Peter breaks down in tears when he realizes it.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Trial before Pilate: A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 provides rare physical evidence that Pontius Pilate really governed Judea under Emperor Tiberius.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Crucifixion: It took place at Golgotha, which means place of the skull, outside the walls of Jerusalem, which is today inside the old city.
Holy Week, as Mark's Gospel tells it.Burial in the tomb: Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, asked Pilate for the body and provided his own unused tomb, cut into rock.

Anniversary words, by number of years.Quinquennial: It comes from Latin quinque and annus, five and year, and it describes something that happens every five years, or lasts that long.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Decennial: The US census is decennial, held every ten years since 1790, and it is required by the Constitution to decide House seats.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Vicennial: It comes from Latin viginti, twenty, and is rare in everyday use, though it appears in old records of anniversaries.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Centennial: Philadelphia hosted the 1876 Centennial Exposition for the US's 100th birthday, where the Statue of Liberty's torch and the telephone were shown.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Sesquicentennial: Sesqui means one and a half, so this is one and a half centuries, and the word is a classic crossword and spelling-bee challenge.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Bicentennial: The US marked this in 1976 with huge celebrations, including a grand tall-ships parade into New York Harbor.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Semiquincentennial: The US marks this in 2026 for its founding in 1776, and it is one of the longest words on the list.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Tercentennial: Harvard marked this in 1936, three hundred years after it was founded in 1636, making it the oldest US university.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Quincentennial: The year 1992 marked this milestone for Columbus's voyage, with a world's fair in Seville and an Olympics in Barcelona.
Anniversary words, by number of years.Millennial: It also names the generation that reached adulthood around the year 2000, though the word first meant a thousand-year period.

Discoveries about how our bodies work.Hooke names the cell: Looking at cork under a microscope in Micrographia, he thought the cells looked like monks' rooms.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.Leeuwenhoek sees sperm cells: The Dutch cloth merchant built his own microscopes and called the tiny creatures 'animalcules'.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.Mendel's pea genetics: The Augustinian friar's work on peas was ignored until about 1900, when others rediscovered his laws of heredity.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.Blood types (A, B, O): Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO system and won the Nobel Prize in 1930, making safe transfusions possible.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.The word vitamine coined: Casimir Funk coined it, and the final 'e' was later dropped when not all vitamins were found to be amines.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.Insulin isolated: Banting and Best sold the insulin patent to the University of Toronto for one dollar each.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.DNA double helix: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 helped Watson and Crick, and they published in Nature in April 1953.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.First IVF baby born: Louise Brown was born in Oldham, England, on 25 July 1978, and the pioneers behind the process later won a Nobel Prize.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.Bacteria cause stomach ulcers: Barry Marshall drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori to prove it, and shared the 2005 Nobel Prize with Robin Warren.
Discoveries about how our bodies work.First gapless human genome: The Telomere-to-Telomere consortium filled the last gaps left in the original genome.

Countries by total area.Greece: The country has about 6,000 islands and islets, roughly 200 inhabited, and no point on the mainland is more than about 137 km from the sea.
Countries by total area.Japan: Thousands of islands make up the country, and it is about 70 percent mountains, so most people live on a small share of the land.
Countries by total area.France: The figure includes overseas regions such as French Guiana; mainland France alone is about 550,000 km².
Countries by total area.Egypt: About 95 percent of Egyptians live along the Nile on a sliver of land, while most of the country is desert.
Countries by total area.Mexico: It has more Spanish speakers than any other country, and its name comes from the Mexica, the Aztec people.
Countries by total area.India: Since 2023 it has had the world's largest population, over 1.4 billion people, and it is the largest democracy.
Countries by total area.Australia: It is the only country that is also a continent, and it is close in area to the lower 48 US states.
Countries by total area.Brazil: It takes up nearly half of South America and borders every country on the continent except Chile and Ecuador.
Countries by total area.Canada: By many counts it has more lakes than the rest of the world combined, and the world's longest coastline.
Countries by total area.Russia: Spanning 11 time zones, it is larger than the surface area of Pluto.

The famous numbers behind these food fac.Beef patties in a Big Mac: Created by Jim Delligatti in Pennsylvania in 1967, the Big Mac was later famous for a jingle that challenged people to recite its ingredients.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Most Michelin stars possible: Three stars means exceptional cuisine worth a special journey; the guide began in 1900 as a motorist's handbook from the tire company.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Jack Daniel's 'Old No.': The origin of the 7 remains a mystery, with several theories, though the whiskey comes from Lynchburg, Tennessee.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.KFC's herbs and spices: Colonel Sanders's recipe is reputedly locked in a vault in Louisville.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Dr Pepper's flavors: The drink is older than Coca-Cola, created in Waco, Texas, in 1885.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Bénédictine's herbs and spices: A French herbal liqueur created by Alexandre Le Grand in 1863, it claims monastic roots in Fécamp.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Baskin-Robbins flavors slogan: There is one for every day of the month; the chain was founded in 1945 in Glendale, California.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Jägermeister's botanicals: This German herbal liqueur's stag logo refers to St. Hubert, patron saint of hunters.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Heinz 'varieties' (slogan): Henry Heinz reportedly picked the number because he liked five and seven, though the company made far more than 57 products.
The famous numbers behind these food fac.Plants in Chartreuse: Made by Carthusian monks in France, its full recipe is reputedly known to just two monks at a time.

Greek letters in alphabetical order.Alpha (α): Its name, joined with beta, gave us the word alphabet. It also means "first" in science and sport: alpha particles, alpha wolves, alpha testing.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Gamma (γ): Gamma rays, the most energetic form of light, are named for it. It comes from the Phoenician word for "camel", as the letter was a stylized camel's neck.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Delta (δ): The capital form stands for change in math and science. The river-mouth landform is named for its triangle shape, as in the Nile Delta.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Epsilon (ε): The name means "simple e" in Greek, to tell it from a letter that sounded alike. In math, it means a tiny quantity that can be as small as you like.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Theta (θ): Mathematicians use it for an unknown angle. It also names a slow brain-wave rhythm linked with drowsiness, memory and deep relaxation.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Lambda (λ): Physicists use it for wavelength. Lambda calculus, from the 1930s, is the idea behind anonymous functions in many programming languages.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Pi (π): Its value, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, is about 3.14159. Computers have calculated it to trillions of digits.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Sigma (σ): The capital form means "sum" in math. The small form is the usual symbol for standard deviation, the spread of data.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Phi (φ): The small form often stands for the golden ratio, about 1.618. It's also the symbol that sound-wave and physics notation use for phase angles.
Greek letters in alphabetical order.Omega (ω): The last Greek letter stands for the ohm, the unit of electrical resistance, and has come to mean "the end" in "alpha and omega".

Online worlds and multiplayer games.MUD1: Written by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle at Essex University, this text adventure for many players gave the whole MUD genre its name.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.Habitat: Lucasfilm Games's graphic online world ran on a Commodore 64 over the phone line, and it gave the word "avatar" its use for an online persona.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.Ultima Online: Origin Systems' fantasy world, whose creator Richard Garriott is credited with coining the term MMORPG, let players hold jobs, build homes and fight each other.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.EverQuest: Nicknamed "EverCrack" by some players for being so addictive, it let thousands of players explore a 3D fantasy world, from Sony Online.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.RuneScape: This British fantasy world began in a web browser, created by Andrew Gower of Jagex. A 2007 version, Old School RuneScape, is still played.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.Second Life: Linden Lab's virtual world lets residents build, own land and trade with a currency, the Linden dollar, that can be exchanged for real money.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.World of Warcraft: Blizzard's fantasy game peaked at over 12 million subscribers in 2010. Its Warcraft universe goes back to a strategy game from 1994.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.Club Penguin: Kids' penguin world, launched by a small team, was bought by Disney in 2007 for $350 million, and lasted until 2017 in its original form.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.Roblox: Created by David Baszucki and Erik Cassel, the platform's games are made by users, and it has well over 70 million daily players.
Online worlds and multiplayer games.League of Legends: Riot Games' free multiplayer arena game was inspired by Defense of the Ancients, a Warcraft III mod, and its world championship fills stadiums.

European cities by population (city prop.Vatican City: Vatican City is the world's smallest state, and its population is mostly clergy and Swiss Guards.
European cities by population (city prop.Monaco: Monaco is the most densely populated country, and it's famous for its casino and a Grand Prix through its streets.
European cities by population (city prop.Reykjavík: Reykjavík is the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state, and it heats many buildings with geothermal water.
European cities by population (city prop.Lisbon: Lisbon is one of Europe's oldest cities, older than Rome, and it was largely rebuilt after an earthquake in 1755.
European cities by population (city prop.Amsterdam: Amsterdam has more bikes than residents, and most of its canals were dug in the 17th century.
European cities by population (city prop.Prague: Prague's old town escaped major bombing in World War II, and it has a medieval astronomical clock still working.
European cities by population (city prop.Paris: Paris has grown beyond its city limits; its metropolitan area is much bigger, with over 12 million people.
European cities by population (city prop.Rome: Rome has been home to a million people since ancient times, and it contains an entire country inside it.
European cities by population (city prop.Berlin: Berlin is the largest city in Germany, and it has more bridges than Venice.
European cities by population (city prop.London: London is the largest city in Europe west of Moscow, and Londinium was founded by the Romans in AD 43.

Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Count Dracula: Bram Stoker's vampire was inspired partly by Transylvanian folklore, and the novel was written as a series of diaries and letters.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Peter Pan: The boy who would not grow up first appeared in a book for adults, 'The Little White Bird', before he got his own play and novel.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Tarzan: Edgar Rice Burroughs' ape-raised hero first swung into a pulp magazine, and the character later appeared in more than 200 films.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Zorro: The masked swordsman first appeared in a serial story and his black costume and Z-shaped mark helped inspire Batman.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Winnie-the-Pooh: A. A. Milne named his bear after a real Canadian black bear, Winnipeg, at the London Zoo, as well as his son's toy.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Conan the Barbarian: Robert E. Howard's barbarian first appeared in the pulp magazine Weird Tales, and the author never lived to see the swords-and-sorcery craze he started.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.James Bond: Ian Fleming wrote Casino Royale at his Jamaican estate, Goldeneye, and he named the hero after an ornithologist's book on birds.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Paddington Bear: Michael Bond's bear came from darkest Peru with a label reading 'Please look after this bear', and he adores marmalade sandwiches.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Jack Ryan: Tom Clancy's analyst-turned-hero first appeared in The Hunt for Red October, a novel first rejected by many publishers and later hugely popular.
Fictional icons, by first appearance in.Katniss Everdeen: Suzanne Collins' heroine volunteers to take her sister's place in a deadly televised contest, and her story was inspired by reality TV and Greek myth.

Milestones of blood transfusion.Denys transfuses lamb's blood: The French physician tried to cure a young boy's fever with lamb's blood, and the boy survived, though later attempts failed and the practice was banned.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Blundell's human-to-human: The British obstetrician transfused human blood to women bleeding after childbirth, using a syringe; some patients survived.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Landsteiner's blood groups: The Austrian scientist found the A, B and O groups, explaining why some transfusions failed, and he won a Nobel Prize for it in 1930.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Cross-matched transfusion: Reuben Ottenberg performed the first transfusion based on matching donor and recipient, which made transfusions much safer.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Citrate lets blood be stored: Adding sodium citrate stopped blood from clotting, so it could be stored for days, making it possible to transfuse in the trenches of World War I.
Milestones of blood transfusion.First hospital blood bank: It opened at Chicago's Cook County Hospital, and its founder Bernard Fantus coined the name 'blood bank'.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Rh factor discovered: Landsteiner and Wiener found this factor using rhesus monkeys, which explained why some babies of Rh-negative mothers became seriously ill.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Plastic blood bags: Flexible plastic bags replaced breakable glass bottles, and they made it easier to separate blood into parts for different patients.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Donated blood tested for HIV: Screening donated blood for the virus began soon after it was identified, and it made transfusions much safer.
Milestones of blood transfusion.Lab-grown red cells transfused: In a trial, volunteers received small amounts of red cells grown from stem cells, to learn how long they last in the body.

Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Armenia: The small, mountainous nation was the first to adopt Christianity as a state religion, in 301, and it is home to the world's oldest known leather shoe.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Georgia: The country is the birthplace of wine, with 8,000-year-old winemaking evidence, and its alphabet is one of only a few unique ones in the world.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Azerbaijan: The country is known as the Land of Fire, because of its natural gas, and its capital, Baku, was an early oil boom city.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Tajikistan: The Pamir mountains cover most of this country, and the highest peak is Ismoil Somoni Peak, formerly Communism Peak.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Kyrgyzstan: Nearly all of this country is mountains, and its name is said to mean 'forty tribes', and it also has the huge lake Issyk-Kul.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Uzbekistan: The country is double landlocked, which means it is surrounded by landlocked countries, and Samarkand was a Silk Road hub.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Turkmenistan: The country's capital has marble buildings, and in the Karakum desert a gas crater has been burning for decades.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Afghanistan: The country is known as the 'graveyard of empires', and it stretches through mountains and the famous Hindu Kush.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Mongolia: It is the least densely populated sovereign country in the world, and Genghis Khan's empire began here.
Central Asian and Caucasus countries by.Kazakhstan: It is the world's largest landlocked country, and the Baikonur Cosmodrome, from which Gagarin launched, lies within it.

Surprising timeline: what came first?.Great Pyramid of Giza built: Built as Khufu's tomb, it stood as the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Rome founded: By legend Romulus founded the city after killing his twin Remus, though Roman scholars only worked out the date centuries later.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Cleopatra's reign begins: She lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Teaching starts at Oxford: Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world, and it was already teaching before the Aztec capital existed.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Tenochtitlan founded: The Aztec capital rose on an island in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways. Mexico City now stands on its ruins.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Machu Picchu built: Built for an Inca emperor with stones cut to fit without mortar, it was never found by the Spanish conquerors.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Harvard founded: America's oldest university predates the United States by 140 years, and is named after a donor, John Harvard.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Ottoman Empire ends: The sultanate was abolished after more than 600 years, and the Republic of Turkey was declared the next year.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.Sliced bread first sold: Otto Rohwedder invented the bread-slicing machine, and the first loaves were sold in Chillicothe, Missouri.
Surprising timeline: what came first?.France's last guillotining: Hamida Djandoubi was the last person executed this way in France, and the death penalty was abolished in 1981.

Percents, decimals and fractions.5%: The word percent comes from the Latin per centum, meaning by the hundred, and the % sign evolved from a scribal shorthand for it.
Percents, decimals and fractions.0.08: Compounding at this rate doubles money in about nine years by the rule of 72, which is why small percentages matter over time.
Percents, decimals and fractions.1/10: Decimal comes from the Latin for tenth, and the metric prefix deci- also means one tenth, as in a decilitre.
Percents, decimals and fractions.15%: This is the usual restaurant tip in the US. A quick way to find it is to take 10% and then add half of that again.
Percents, decimals and fractions.1/5: A fifth of a gallon was the traditional US size of a liquor bottle, which is why spirits are still called a fifth.
Percents, decimals and fractions.0.25: A quarter is why the US 25-cent coin has that name, and a quarter-hour is another everyday use of this fraction.
Percents, decimals and fractions.1/3: Its decimal repeats forever, which happens whenever the denominator has prime factors other than 2 and 5, so a third can never be written exactly.
Percents, decimals and fractions.45%: A 45% discount leaves you paying 55% of the original price, so the quick trick is to take the number off from 100.
Percents, decimals and fractions.0.6: This is close to the reciprocal of the golden ratio, which is about 0.618, a number artists and mathematicians love.
Percents, decimals and fractions.3/4: Three quarters is the time signature of the waltz, with three beats to the bar, the dance's famous one-two-three rhythm.

How many times a day, on average.Poop: One a day is common, but healthy habits range anywhere from three times a day to three times a week.
How many times a day, on average.Pee: A bladder holds roughly 400 to 500 ml, and the urge to go starts when it is only about a third full.
How many times a day, on average.Fart: A person produces roughly half a liter of intestinal gas a day, most of it odorless nitrogen, hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
How many times a day, on average.Shed a scalp hair: A typical head has around 100,000 hairs, so losing this many each day is normal and is balanced by new growth.
How many times a day, on average.Swallow: You swallow even in your sleep, though less often, and each swallow uses around 30 muscles in your mouth and throat.
How many times a day, on average.Blink: Babies blink far less than adults, and staring at screens makes us blink less too, which is why eyes feel dry.
How many times a day, on average.Breathe: Together that moves more than 10,000 liters of air through your lungs, mostly without your ever thinking about it.
How many times a day, on average.Heartbeat: Over a lifetime that adds up to about 2.5 billion beats, from a muscle that never takes a day off.
How many times a day, on average.Shed a skin cell: The outer skin layer is replaced roughly monthly, and a good share of household dust is made of shed skin.
How many times a day, on average.Make a red blood cell: Bone marrow makes roughly two million of these every second, replacing the ones that wear out after about four months.

Top speeds of famous flying machines.Wright Flyer: Orville's first flight on 17 December 1903 lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres, shorter than a jumbo jet's wingspan.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Hindenburg airship: Filled with hydrogen, this German airship burned over New Jersey in 1937, killing 36 people and ending the age of passenger airships.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Sopwith Camel: Named for the hump over its guns, this WWI fighter was credited with shooting down more than 1,200 enemy aircraft.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Cessna 172: It is the most-produced aircraft ever, with well over 40,000 built since the 1950s, and it is where many pilots learn to fly.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Spitfire Mk I: Its elliptical wing and Rolls-Royce Merlin engine helped it hold the line against the Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Messerschmitt Me 262: This German jet was the first operational jet fighter, entering service in 1944, but it came too late to change the war.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.Concorde: It flew London to New York in under three and a half hours, and its nose drooped on landing so pilots could see the runway.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.MiG-25 Foxbat: In 1976 a Soviet pilot named Viktor Belenko landed one in Japan, defecting and giving Western analysts their first close look.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.SR-71 Blackbird: It could outrun missiles by simply speeding up, and in 1974 one flew from New York to London in under two hours.
Top speeds of famous flying machines.North American X-15: A rocket plane dropped from a B-52 bomber, it reached the edge of space, and Neil Armstrong flew it before Apollo.

Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Tritium: This hydrogen isotope is used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials and emergency exit signs.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Lead-210: A product of the radon decay chain, it can be used to date sediments from the last century or so.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Carbon-14: Willard Libby won the 1960 Nobel Prize for radiocarbon dating, which works on things up to about 50,000 years old.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Chlorine-36: It can date groundwater and rock surfaces exposed to cosmic rays, and nuclear tests in the 1950s left a spike in the record.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Beryllium-10: Cosmic rays make it in the atmosphere, and ice cores that hold it help scientists track the Sun's past activity.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Uranium-235: The fissile isotope that powers reactors and the first bomb used on Hiroshima makes up only 0.7 percent of natural uranium.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Potassium-40: The same radioactive element is in bananas, and its decay to argon dates volcanic rocks, including those near early human fossils.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Uranium-238: It makes up over 99 percent of natural uranium, and its decay to lead dated the Earth to about 4.5 billion years.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Thorium-232: It is about three times more common in Earth's crust than uranium, and it is considered as an alternative reactor fuel.
Rock-dating clocks: half-lives of isotop.Rubidium-87: It decays into strontium-87, and the rubidium-strontium method dates the oldest rocks and meteorites.

How long food keeps safely.Cooked food left out: Food safety experts call roughly 5 to 60 degrees Celsius the danger zone, where bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes.
How long food keeps safely.Raw chicken in the fridge: Washing raw chicken is discouraged, since splashing can spread Salmonella and Campylobacter around the kitchen; cooking to 74 °C kills them.
How long food keeps safely.Leftovers in the fridge: Rice is a classic leftover danger: spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and can produce toxins if the rice sits at room temperature.
How long food keeps safely.Opened milk: Milk sours as bacteria turn lactose into lactic acid, which is also why spoiled milk smells sharp and curdles when heated.
How long food keeps safely.Raw eggs in the fridge: An eggshell has thousands of tiny pores; US eggs are washed and refrigerated, while in much of Europe unwashed eggs sit unchilled on shelves.
How long food keeps safely.Butter in the fridge: Butter is about 80 percent fat and low in water, which slows bacterial growth; salted butter lasts longer and freezing extends it greatly.
How long food keeps safely.Ground beef, frozen: Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the whole meat, which is why burgers must be cooked through while a steak's center can stay pink.
How long food keeps safely.Steaks, frozen: Food kept frozen at -18 °C stays safe indefinitely; the time limits are about quality, since freezer burn dries out and dulls the flavor.
How long food keeps safely.Low-acid canned food: Low-acid canning needs a pressure canner reaching about 116 °C to destroy botulism spores; plain boiling water isn't hot enough.
How long food keeps safely.Honey: Honey's low water and high sugar content starve microbes, so it rarely spoils; if it crystallizes, gentle warming turns it runny again.

Plant pioneers by year of birth.Theophrastus: Aristotle's student, called the father of botany, wrote Enquiry into Plants and described around 500 kinds.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Dioscorides: A Greek physician serving in Nero's army, Dioscorides wrote De Materia Medica, a herbal that was a medical authority for some 1,500 years.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Carl Linnaeus: Linnaeus gave us two-part Latin names such as Homo sapiens, used consistently in his 1753 Species Plantarum.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Joseph Banks: Banks sailed with Captain Cook on the Endeavour, gathered thousands of plants, and later guided Kew Gardens; the genus Banksia honors him.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Alexander von Humboldt: Humboldt climbed Chimborazo and noticed how plant zones change with altitude, an early glimpse of ecology and climate zones.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Gregor Mendel: Mendel's pea-plant crosses in a monastery garden revealed the laws of heredity, but his work was ignored until after 1900.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Luther Burbank: Burbank bred hundreds of plant varieties, including a potato that grew into the Russet Burbank, still widely used for french fries.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.George Washington Carver: Carver urged farmers to rotate peanuts and sweet potatoes with cotton to restore the soil, and promoted hundreds of uses for peanuts.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Barbara McClintock: McClintock discovered jumping genes in maize in the 1940s, and was awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Medicine alone, decades afterward.
Plant pioneers by year of birth.Norman Borlaug: Borlaug's high-yield, disease-resistant wheat sparked the Green Revolution, earning him the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for helping feed millions.

How many different values each can hold.One bit: The word 'bit' is short for 'binary digit', a term credited to statistician John Tukey in the 1940s.
How many different values each can hold.One hex digit: Hex uses 0-9 and A-F, and each digit maps to exactly four bits, so it makes binary compact to read.
How many different values each can hold.One byte: Eight bits make a byte, and 256 values is why 255 turns up everywhere, such as in color channels.
How many different values each can hold.A 4-digit PIN: Only 10,000 four-digit PINs exist, and many people choose '1234' or birth years, making guessing easier.
How many different values each can hold.A 16-bit integer: Signed 16-bit numbers run from minus 32,768 to 32,767, a limit that has caused real bugs in old software and games.
How many different values each can hold.A 6-digit login code: One in a million; authenticator apps change these codes about every 30 seconds so guessing is impractical.
How many different values each can hold.Colors in 24-bit True Color: 256 levels each of red, green and blue gives about 16.7 million colors, possibly more than the eye can distinguish.
How many different values each can hold.IPv4 addresses: The top-level supply of these 32-bit addresses ran out in 2011, driving the adoption of IPv6 and address sharing.
How many different values each can hold.A 64-bit integer: Moving from 32-bit to 64-bit let computers address vastly more memory than the old 4 GB limit.
How many different values each can hold.IPv6 addresses: With 128-bit addresses, there are trillions of trillions of trillions of options, so the supply should never run out.

Asian car brands, by founding year.Suzuki: Began in 1909 as a maker of weaving looms, and only later moved on to motorcycles and cars.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Mazda: Started in 1920 as a cork maker. Its name nods to both founder Jujiro Matsuda and Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian god of wisdom.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Nissan: The name is a contraction of Nihon Sangyo, meaning 'Japan Industries'. Its Datsun brand was sold worldwide before the switch.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Kia: South Korea's oldest carmaker began by making steel tubing and bicycle parts. Its name loosely means 'rising out of Asia'.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Subaru: The Japanese name for the Pleiades star cluster, which is why its logo shows six stars.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Hyundai Motor: Part of a huge Korean conglomerate. 'Hyundai' means 'modernity' in Korean.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Acura: Honda's luxury brand, launched in 1986, was the first Japanese luxury marque, and it debuted in the United States.
Asian car brands, by founding year.Lexus: Toyota's luxury arm launched in 1989 with the LS 400 sedan, built to challenge Mercedes-Benz and BMW on quality.
Asian car brands, by founding year.BYD Auto: Grew out of a battery maker, with Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway investing in 2008. It now rivals Tesla in electric-car sales.
Asian car brands, by founding year.NIO: The Chinese electric-car maker is known for swappable batteries: its stations can swap a drained pack for a full one in minutes.

Dinosaurs on the scale.Microraptor: A four-winged, feathered dinosaur from China about 120 million years ago, with flight feathers on its legs as well as arms.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Compsognathus: Roughly turkey-sized and found in Late Jurassic Germany, it was long thought the smallest dinosaur and is among the first discovered.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Velociraptor: The real animal was about turkey-sized and feathered, much smaller and fluffier than the scaly beasts of Jurassic Park.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Deinonychus: Its 1960s discovery led John Ostrom to argue that dinosaurs were active, warm-blooded and related to birds, igniting a 'dinosaur renaissance'.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Utahraptor: The largest known 'raptor', it was named after the US state where its fossils were found. It had a huge sickle claw on each foot.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Parasaurolophus: Its long, hollow, curved crest probably worked like a horn, producing deep resonant calls that carried through the forest.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Tyrannosaurus rex: Its bite ranks among the strongest of any land animal, and was powerful enough to crush bone.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Diplodocus: A famous cast of this dinosaur, 'Dippy', greeted visitors at London's Natural History Museum for decades, tail swooping overhead.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Brachiosaurus: Its forelegs were longer than its hind legs, giving it a giraffe-like posture, with a neck that held its head very high.
Dinosaurs on the scale.Argentinosaurus: Known only from fragmentary bones found in Patagonia, so its size is estimated by scaling up from relatives.

US states by population.Wyoming: The least populous state, Wyoming, has fewer people than many big-city suburbs, and it was first to give women the vote as a territory.
US states by population.Oregon: Oregon was settled by pioneers on the Oregon Trail, and Portland is the home of Powell's, one of the biggest independent bookstores.
US states by population.Colorado: Colorado has more than 50 peaks over 14,000 feet, and Denver sits exactly one mile above sea level.
US states by population.Massachusetts: Massachusetts holds Harvard, MIT and the site of Plymouth, and it was where the Revolution's first shots were fired in 1775.
US states by population.Michigan: Michigan touches four of the five Great Lakes, and no point in the state is more than about 85 miles from one.
US states by population.Pennsylvania: Pennsylvania's Philadelphia hosted the signing of both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.
US states by population.New York: New York State is home to the nation's largest city, but most of its land is farm, forest and mountains upstate.
US states by population.Florida: Florida's population has surged in recent decades, and it has more miles of coastline than any other state except Alaska.
US states by population.Texas: Texas passed New York in population in the 1990s, and it's the only state that was once an independent republic.
US states by population.California: California has more people than all of Canada, and if it were a country its economy would rank among the world's largest.

Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Emily Brontë: Emily Brontë's only novel, Wuthering Heights, was first published under the male pen name Ellis Bell, and critics didn't know what to make of it.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Harper Lee: Harper Lee published To Kill a Mockingbird in 1960 and Go Set a Watchman in 2015, which was actually written earlier.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Franz Kafka: Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unfinished novels, but Brod refused, giving us The Trial, The Castle and Amerika.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.F. Scott Fitzgerald: Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby sold poorly in his lifetime, and his fifth novel, The Last Tycoon, was left unfinished at his death.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Jane Austen: Austen published novels anonymously, as 'By a Lady', and her last two, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, came out after she died.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Raymond Chandler: Chandler created the detective Philip Marlowe, and he is credited with shaping the hardboiled style of crime fiction.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Thomas Hardy: Hardy stopped writing novels after the harsh criticism of Jude the Obscure and turned to poetry for the rest of his life.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Charles Dickens: Dickens published most of his novels in monthly or weekly installments, which is why the plots are full of cliffhangers.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Agatha Christie: Christie is the best-selling novelist of all time, and her play The Mousetrap has run in London since 1952.
Authors, by how many novels they wrote.Barbara Cartland: Cartland wrote romances, dictated to a secretary while reclining on a sofa, and she once set a record with 23 novels in a year.

When Google launched these.Google Search: Google Search began as a Stanford project called BackRub, and the name Google plays on googol, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
When Google launched these.AdWords: AdWords began with about 350 advertisers and became the main source of Google's revenue, now a multibillion-dollar business.
When Google launched these.Google News: Google News used algorithms instead of human editors to group stories, and was built after the September 11 attacks.
When Google launched these.Gmail: Gmail launched on April Fools' Day with 1 gigabyte of storage, which sounded like a joke when rivals offered a few megabytes.
When Google launched these.Google Earth: Earth began as Keyhole's technology, which Google bought, and it lets you fly anywhere on the planet from your desk.
When Google launched these.Street View: Street View cars carry cameras that have photographed millions of kilometers of roads, and they sometimes capture odd scenes.
When Google launched these.Chrome: Chrome was announced with a comic book explaining its design, and it became the world's most-used browser.
When Google launched these.Google+: Google's social network was meant to compete with Facebook, and it was shut down for consumers in 2019.
When Google launched these.Google Photos: Photos offered free unlimited storage for years, and used machine learning to find faces and scenes in pictures.
When Google launched these.Bard: Bard was Google's answer to ChatGPT; it was renamed Gemini within about a year of launch.

After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Heart rate drops: Nicotine pushes up your pulse, and it starts falling to normal soon after the last cigarette.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Blood carbon monoxide normal: Carbon monoxide from smoke binds to blood more strongly than oxygen does, and it clears within hours.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Taste and smell improve: Damaged nerve endings start regrowing, so food begins to taste better and smells sharper.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Breathing gets easier: Bronchial tubes begin to relax, and breathing becomes easier.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Circulation improves: Blood flow in the limbs improves, and walking and exercise get gradually easier.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Coughing eases: Tiny hair-like cilia in the lungs recover, helping sweep out mucus and lowering infection risk.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Heart disease risk halved: Your risk of coronary heart disease is around half that of a smoker, after just one year.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Stroke risk like a nonsmoker: Stroke risk can fall to that of a never-smoker within a few years of stopping.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Lung cancer risk halved: The risk of dying of lung cancer is around half that of a continuing smoker, and keeps falling.
After your last cigarette: benefits in o.Heart risk like a nonsmoker: Fifteen years on, heart disease risk is about the same as for someone who never smoked.

Spans of years.Biennium: Biennium comes from Latin for two years, and it's used for budgets, such as US state legislative budgets.
Spans of years.Olympiad: An Olympiad was the four-year period between ancient Greek Olympic Games, and the Greeks used it to count years.
Spans of years.Lustrum: A lustrum was a Roman purification ceremony held every five years after the census.
Spans of years.Decade: Decade comes from the Greek deka, meaning ten, and the 1920s decade is often named the Roaring Twenties.
Spans of years.Score: Score for twenty comes from old counting by notches in a stick, and it's used in Lincoln's Four score and seven years ago.
Spans of years.Golden jubilee: Golden jubilee marks 50 years, and it has roots in the biblical Jubilee year, every fiftieth year, when debts were forgiven.
Spans of years.Century: A century is 100 years, from Latin centum, and Romans used the word for army units of 100 men too.
Spans of years.Sesquicentennial: A sesquicentennial marks 150 years, and the word sesqui is Latin for one and a half.
Spans of years.Bicentennial: A bicentennial marks 200 years, and America celebrated its bicentennial in 1976.
Spans of years.Millennium: Millennium comes from Latin mille for thousand and annus for year, and it prompted Y2K worry as 2000 approached.

When these ways of getting around arrive.The wheel: The wheel first appeared in pottery-making, long before it was used on carts. Putting wheels on axles was a much later leap.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Hot-air balloon flight: The Montgolfier brothers' balloon carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster in 1783. The first human passengers went up soon after.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Steam locomotive: Richard Trevithick's engine hauled iron and passengers in Wales. It wasn't a commercial success, but it proved steam could pull a train.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Bicycle (the draisine): Karl von Drais's wooden two-wheeler had no pedals, and riders pushed along with their feet. It was nicknamed the hobby-horse.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Motorcycle: Daimler and Maybach put a petrol engine in a wooden frame, creating the first motorcycle. Daimler's son rode it on a test trip.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Petrol-powered car: Karl Benz's three-wheeled Motorwagen was the first practical petrol car. His wife Bertha took it on the first long road trip in 1888.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Powered aeroplane: Orville and Wilbur Wright's first flight at Kitty Hawk lasted 12 seconds. They covered about 120 feet.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Practical helicopter: Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 was the first successful single-rotor helicopter. It had to be tethered during early tests.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Hovercraft: Christopher Cockerell tested the principle with a cat-food tin, a coffee tin and a hairdryer. His craft crossed the English Channel in 1959.
When these ways of getting around arrive.Segway: This two-wheeled scooter balances itself using gyroscopes and tilt sensors. Inventor Dean Kamen hoped it would reshape cities.

Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Street brawl in Verona: Verona is a real Italian city, and it has a Juliet's house with a balcony that draws tourists.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Romeo crashes a Capulet party: At the ball Romeo and Juliet's first conversation forms a shared 14-line sonnet.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.The balcony scene: In Shakespeare's text Juliet appears above at a window, and the word balcony is not used.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.A secret wedding: Friar Laurence marries them in secret, and he is a herbalist whose potions drive the plot.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Tybalt kills Mercutio: Mercutio's dying curse A plague o' both your houses! is among the play's most famous lines.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Romeo kills Tybalt: Prince Escalus banishes Romeo rather than executing him for killing Tybalt.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Romeo is banished: Mantua is a real Italian city, and the plan fails because Romeo never receives the friar's letter.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Juliet takes the potion: Shakespeare based the play on Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem and older Italian tales, and the potion mimics death.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Romeo drinks poison: Romeo buys the poison from an apothecary, an illegal act, and swallows it believing Juliet dead.
Romeo and Juliet, in story order.Juliet stabs herself: Juliet uses Romeo's dagger and says O happy dagger, this is thy sheath.

World War I, in order.Franz Ferdinand shot: The Austrian archduke was shot in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, who got his chance when the royal driver took a wrong turn and stalled the car.
World War I, in order.Germany invades Belgium: Germany's chancellor dismissed the treaty guaranteeing Belgian neutrality as a scrap of paper, and Britain declared war in response.
World War I, in order.Christmas truce: Soldiers on the Western Front sang carols, swapped gifts and, reportedly, kicked a football around no man's land; commanders later worked to stop a repeat.
World War I, in order.Gallipoli landings: The Allied attempt to seize the Dardanelles failed after months of fighting; Australians and New Zealanders now mark ANZAC Day on April 25.
World War I, in order.Lusitania sunk: A German U-boat sank the liner off Ireland, killing nearly 1,200 people including over 120 Americans, which hardened US opinion against Germany.
World War I, in order.Battle of Verdun begins: Lasting about ten months, it became a symbol of French resistance and left roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides combined.
World War I, in order.Battle of the Somme begins: On the first day the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties, its worst single day ever; tanks made their debut later in the battle.
World War I, in order.US enters the war: Woodrow Wilson asked Congress to make the world safe for democracy after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram surfaced.
World War I, in order.Armistice: The ceasefire was signed in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiegne and took effect at 11 a.m. on the eleventh day of the eleventh month.
World War I, in order.Treaty of Versailles: It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors five years to the day after the assassination in Sarajevo, and its reparations clauses fed German resentment.

Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Cook crosses Antarctic Circle: Captain James Cook's ship crossed the Antarctic Circle, but ice blocked him from seeing land and he thought no habitable continent lay beyond.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Bellingshausen sights ice: The Russian expedition is often credited with the first sighting of the Antarctic continent.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Ross Ice Shelf found: James Clark Ross found this huge floating ice sheet, roughly the size of France.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Amundsen at the Pole: The Norwegian explorer reached the Pole first, using dogs and skis, in December 1911.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Scott at the Pole: Robert Falcon Scott arrived about a month later and found the Norwegian flag; his party died on the return.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Endurance trapped: Ernest Shackleton's ship was crushed by ice, and all 28 men survived after a heroic journey.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Byrd flies over the Pole: Pilot Bernt Balchen flew Admiral Byrd's Ford trimotor across the Pole and back.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Trans-Antarctic crossing: Vivian Fuchs's team used snow vehicles, with Edmund Hillary's support, to complete a crossing of about 3,400 kilometres.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.Antarctic Treaty signed: Twelve countries agreed to use the continent only for peaceful science, with no military activity and no mining.
Antarctic firsts, and a penguin film.March of the Penguins: The French documentary about emperor penguins won the Oscar for best documentary feature.
